summary: Clarifies when Node-ID based RSVP Hello messages are used. Their use is implied in cases such as when data and control planes are separated or when traffic engineering links are unnumbered, and when failure detection happens by other means. It is a standards-track clarification.

eli5.summary: Two routers send short hello messages to check each other is still there. This explains which address the hellos should be sent to and from, so the check works in tricky setups.

questions: what is a node-id based rsvp hello
when must rsvp use node-id hello sessions
subtitle: Spelling out when routers should run RSVP Hello sessions between node addresses instead of link addresses.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE routers use Hello messages to notice when a neighbor's signaling has failed, but the use of Hello sessions tied to the node rather than to a link was only implied, and that left the behavior unclear.
tldr.mechanism: A node puts its own Node-ID (its TE router ID) in the source address and the neighbor's Node-ID in the destination address of the Hello packet, and replies using the Node-ID the packet was addressed to.
tldr.outcome: In several listed cases a node MUST run Node-ID based Hello sessions. The change is backward compatible with RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

today: RFC 4558 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It formalizes Node-ID based Hello sessions for both MPLS and GMPLS capable nodes.

sections.title: Why Node-ID Hellos Need Clarifying
sections.content:
The RSVP Hello message exchange was introduced in RFC 3209. RFC 3473 extended its use to support RSVP Graceful Restart for Generalized MPLS (GMPLS).

GMPLS separates the control plane from the data plane. Control information travels over a control network whose end-points are IP capable and may be physically or logically disjoint from the data links they control. As a result, Hello messages are not terminated on the data links' interfaces, even when some of those are numbered. They end at the control channel end-points, which may be identified by the value assigned to the hosting node, the Node-ID.

That is why using Hello for Graceful Restart created a need to clarify how Node-ID based Hello sessions behave.
sections.eli5: When the control wires and the data wires are separate, the hello check has to go to the control side. This document says clearly how to address it there.

sections.title: Node-ID and the Two Kinds of Hello Session
sections.content:
A Node-ID is the TE Router ID as advertised in the Router Address TLV for OSPF and the Traffic Engineering Router ID TLV for IS-IS. For IPv6 it is the Router_IPv6_Address for OSPFv3 and the IPv6 TE Router_ID for IS-IS.

A Node-ID based Hello session is one in which the local and remote Node-IDs are used in the source and destination fields of the Hello packet. An Interface bounded Hello session instead uses the local and remote addresses of the interface in question.
sections.eli5: One kind of hello is addressed to the whole house. The other is addressed to one particular door.

sections.title: Establishing a Node-ID Based Session
sections.content:
A node that wants a Node-ID based session sends a Hello message with its own Node-ID in the source IP address field. It also puts the neighbor's Node-ID in the destination address field of the IP packet.

When a node receives a Hello whose destination address is its local Node-ID as advertised in the IGP-TE topology, it MUST use its Node-ID when replying. Nodes MUST make sure the Node-IDs used in Hello messages are those contained in the IGP-TE topology.

A node can run only one Node-ID based Hello session per IGP instance (that is, per Node-ID pair) with its neighbor.
sections.eli5: You write your own house name as the sender and the neighbor's house name as the receiver. The neighbor answers using the house name you wrote on the envelope.

sections.title: When a Node-ID Session Is Required
sections.content:
The RFC says Node-ID based sessions are optimal for detecting signaling adjacency failure in several situations: when link failure detection is done by some means other than Hello (such as BFD) and there is more than one link between two nodes, when all interfaces between two nodes are unnumbered, and in an optical network with single or multiple numbered or unnumbered control channels.

Therefore, a node MUST run Node-ID based Hello sessions for RSVP-TE signaling adjacency failure detection when link failure detection is done by other means, when all interfaces between a pair of nodes are unnumbered, or in a GMPLS network with data and control plane separation.

If it is useful to tell signaling adjacency failures apart from link failures, Node-ID based sessions can co-exist with interface bound Hellos. They can also co-exist when a pair of nodes share both numbered and unnumbered TE links.
sections.eli5: If there are many roads between two towns, or the roads have no names, it is simpler to check on the town itself than on each road.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The procedure is backward compatible with both RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. Under RFC 3209 the Hello mechanism is meant for immediate neighbors and Hello messages are by default sent between direct RSVP neighbors. This document does not change that, because it uses the IPv4/IPv6 source address of the sending node as the local node_id and the destination address of the neighbor as the remote node_id.

TTL and Hop Limit setting and processing are unchanged. Hello processing for State Recovery from Section 9.3 of RFC 3473, including the RESTART_CAP object, is also not modified.
sections.eli5: Nothing about how old equipment behaves has to change. This only explains how to address the hellos.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document does not modify or extend the Hello exchange between immediate RSVP neighbors, it introduces no new security considerations. The considerations of RFC 3209 remain relevant.

RSVP message security is described in RFC 2747, which provides Hello message integrity and authentication of the Node-ID ownership.
sections.eli5: The way hellos are protected stays the same, and it also confirms that a node really owns the house name it uses.
